cards.term: Who first tried to give classification a scientific basis?
On what basis did Aristotle classify plants into trees, shrubs and herbs?
Into which two groups did Aristotle divide animals?
cards.definition: Those with red blood and those without it

cards.term: Which two kingdoms made up the classification of Linnaeus' time?

cards.text: The two kingdom system did not distinguish between {{c1::eukaryotes and prokaryotes}}, {{c2::unicellular and multicellular}} organisms, and {{c3::photosynthetic (green algae) and non-photosynthetic (fungi)}} organisms.

cards.term: Who proposed the Five Kingdom Classification, and in which year?
Name Whittaker's five kingdoms.
What were Whittaker's main criteria for classification?
cards.definition:
• Cell structure
  • Body organisation
  • Mode of nutrition and reproduction
  • Phylogenetic relationships

cards.text: The three-domain system splits Kingdom {{c1::Monera}} into two domains, giving a {{c2::six}} kingdom classification.

cards.term: In earlier systems, which single character united everything placed under 'Plants'?
Which prokaryotes did earlier systems wrongly group with eukaryotic 'Plants'?
Which unicellular and multicellular algae were placed together in the older system?

cards.text: Fungi have {{c1::chitin}} in their cell walls, while green plants have a {{c2::cellulosic}} cell wall.
Kingdom Protista brought together {{c1::Chlamydomonas and Chlorella}} (earlier in plants) with {{c2::Paramoecium and Amoeba}} (earlier in animals).

cards.term: What does a phylogenetic classification rest on?
Which is the only kingdom with prokaryotic cells?
Which kingdom lacks a nuclear membrane?
Five kingdoms: cell wall
cards.definition: Monera: Non-cellulosic (polysaccharide + amino acid); Protista: Present in some; Fungi: Present, with chitin; Plantae: Present (cellulose); Animalia: Absent

cards.term: Who are the sole members of Kingdom Monera?
Name four extreme habitats where bacteria live.
cards.definition: Hot springs, deserts, snow, deep oceans

cards.text: Bacterial shapes: spherical {{c1::Coccus}}, rod-shaped {{c2::Bacillus}}, comma-shaped {{c3::Vibrium}} and spiral {{c4::Spirillum}}.

cards.term: Figure 2.1 · Bacteria of different shapes
Which group of organisms shows the most extensive metabolic diversity?
What are the two kinds of autotrophic bacteria?
What is the mode of nutrition of the vast majority of bacteria?

cards.text: Archaebacteria: {{c1::halophiles}} live in extreme salty areas, {{c2::thermoacidophiles}} in hot springs, and {{c3::methanogens}} in marshy areas.

cards.term: What lets archaebacteria survive extreme conditions?
cards.definition: A different cell wall structure from other bacteria

cards.term: Where in animals are methanogens found?
cards.definition: In the gut of ruminants, e.g. cows and buffaloes

cards.term: What do methanogens produce from the dung of ruminants?
What two features characterise eubacteria ('true bacteria')?
cards.definition: A rigid cell wall, and a flagellum if motile

cards.term: What is the common name for cyanobacteria?
Which chlorophyll do cyanobacteria share with green plants?
What surrounds cyanobacterial colonies?
What do cyanobacteria often form in polluted water bodies?

cards.text: Some cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called {{c1::heterocysts}}, e.g. {{c2::Nostoc and Anabaena}}.

cards.term: Figure 2.2 · A filamentous blue-green alga, Nostoc
Which substances do chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise for energy?
Chemosynthetic bacteria help recycle which nutrients?
Which bacteria are the most abundant in nature?
What ecological role do most heterotrophic bacteria play?
Give three uses of heterotrophic bacteria.
cards.definition:
• Making curd from milk
  • Producing antibiotics
  • Fixing nitrogen in legume roots

cards.term: Name four diseases caused by bacteria.

cards.text: Bacteria reproduce mainly by {{c1::fission}}; under unfavourable conditions they produce {{c2::spores}}.

cards.term: What sort of sexual reproduction do bacteria show?
cards.definition: A primitive DNA transfer from one bacterium to another

cards.term: Which organisms completely lack a cell wall?
What are the smallest living cells known?
Which kingdom contains all single-celled eukaryotes?
Which five groups does NCERT place under Protista?
cards.definition: Chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds, protozoans

cards.term: What is the main habitat of protists?
How do protists reproduce sexually?
cards.definition: By cell fusion and zygote formation

cards.term: Which organisms make up the chrysophytes?
What are organisms that float passively in water currents called?
How is a diatom cell wall built?
cards.definition: Two thin overlapping shells that fit together like a soap box

cards.term: Why are diatom cell walls indestructible?
What is 'diatomaceous earth'?
cards.definition: Diatom cell wall deposits accumulated over billions of years

cards.term: What is diatomaceous earth used for?
cards.definition: Polishing, and filtration of oils and syrups

cards.term: Who are the chief 'producers' in the oceans?
Where do dinoflagellates mostly live, and how do they get food?
What decides the colour of a dinoflagellate?
cards.definition: The main pigments in its cells

cards.term: What is on the outer surface of a dinoflagellate cell wall?
How are the two flagella of a dinoflagellate arranged?
cards.definition: One longitudinal, one transverse in a furrow between the wall plates

cards.term: Which dinoflagellate causes red tides?
What harm do red tides do?
cards.definition: Their toxins may kill marine animals such as fishes

cards.term: Where are most euglenoids found?
What do euglenoids have instead of a cell wall?
cards.definition: A protein-rich pellicle, which keeps the body flexible

cards.term: What flagella do euglenoids have?
How do euglenoids feed when kept out of sunlight?
Euglenoid pigments are identical to those of which organisms?
Give an example of a euglenoid.
What is the mode of nutrition of slime moulds?
What aggregation do slime moulds form under suitable conditions?
cards.definition: A plasmodium, which can spread over several feet

cards.term: What does the plasmodium form in unfavourable conditions?
cards.definition: Fruiting bodies bearing spores at their tips

cards.term: Name two features of slime mould spores.
cards.definition: True walls; extremely resistant, surviving for many years

cards.term: How are slime mould spores dispersed?
What is the mode of nutrition of protozoans?
cards.definition: All are heterotrophs, living as predators or parasites

cards.term: Protozoans are believed to be primitive relatives of which group?
Name the four major groups of protozoans.
What do amoeboid protozoans use to move and catch prey?
What do marine amoeboid protozoans have on their surface?
Name a parasitic amoeboid protozoan.
Which flagellated protozoan causes sleeping sickness?
How does food reach the gullet of a ciliated protozoan?
cards.definition: Coordinated movement of rows of cilia steers food-laden water in

cards.term: Give an example of a ciliated protozoan.
What feature is shared by all sporozoans?
cards.definition: An infectious spore-like stage in the life cycle

cards.term: Which sporozoan causes malaria?
Figure 2.4 · Name each protist
Which unicellular fungus is used to make bread and beer?
Which fungus causes wheat rust?
Which fungus is a source of antibiotics?
Which fungi are unicellular rather than filamentous?

cards.text: A fungal body is made of long thread-like {{c1::hyphae}}; their network is called the {{c2::mycelium}}.

cards.term: What are coenocytic hyphae?
cards.definition: Continuous tubes filled with multinucleated cytoplasm

cards.term: What divides the hyphae of some fungi into cells?
What are fungal cell walls made of?
What are fungi that absorb soluble organic matter from dead substrates called?

cards.text: Fungi live as symbionts with algae as {{c1::lichens}} and with roots of higher plants as {{c2::mycorrhiza}}.

cards.term: Name three means of vegetative reproduction in fungi.
Name three kinds of asexual spores in fungi.
Name three kinds of sexual spores in fungi.
Where are fungal spores produced?
cards.definition: In distinct structures called fruiting bodies

cards.term: Fungal sexual cycle in order
cards.definition: Plasmogamy (n + n) → karyogamy (2n) → meiosis → haploid spores

cards.term: In the fungal sexual cycle, what is plasmogamy and what is karyogamy?
cards.definition: Plasmogamy: fusion of protoplasms. Karyogamy: fusion of nuclei.

cards.term: What is a dikaryon?
cards.definition: A cell with two nuclei (n + n). The phase is called the dikaryophase.

cards.term: In which fungal classes does a dikaryotic stage occur?
What is the basis for dividing Kingdom Fungi into classes?
cards.definition:
• Morphology of the mycelium
  • Mode of spore formation
  • Fruiting bodies

cards.term: Figure 2.5 · Name each fungus
Where are phycomycetes found?
cards.definition: Aquatic habitats, decaying wood in moist places, or as obligate parasites on plants

cards.term: What kind of mycelium do phycomycetes have?

cards.text: Phycomycetes reproduce asexually by motile {{c1::zoospores}} or non-motile {{c2::aplanospores}}, produced endogenously in a {{c3::sporangium}}.

cards.term: How is a zygospore formed?
What are gametes called when they are similar in morphology?
Which phycomycete is the bread mould?
Which phycomycete is parasitic on mustard?
What is the common name of ascomycetes?
Name a unicellular ascomycete.
What does 'coprophilous' mean?
Where are the asexual spores (conidia) of ascomycetes produced?
Where are ascospores produced?
What are the fruiting bodies of ascomycetes called?
Which ascomycete is used extensively in biochemical and genetic work?
Which edible ascomycetes are considered delicacies?
Name three common forms of basidiomycetes.
Which basidiomycetes are parasites on living plants?
How do basidiomycetes usually reproduce vegetatively?
cards.definition: By fragmentation (asexual spores are generally not found)

cards.term: How does plasmogamy occur in basidiomycetes, which lack sex organs?
cards.definition: Fusion of two vegetative (somatic) cells of different strains

cards.term: Where do karyogamy and meiosis occur in basidiomycetes?
How many basidiospores does a basidium produce?
Are basidiospores produced endogenously or exogenously?
What are the fruiting bodies of basidiomycetes called?
Why are deuteromycetes called imperfect fungi?
cards.definition: Only their asexual or vegetative phases are known

cards.term: Where are deuteromycetes usually moved once their sexual stage is found?
By which spores alone do deuteromycetes reproduce?
What useful role do many deuteromycetes play?
cards.definition: Decomposing litter and helping mineral cycling

cards.term: Ustilago is which kind of fungus?
Which organisms does Kingdom Plantae include?
Name two insectivorous plants.
Name a parasitic plant.
Which five groups make up Kingdom Plantae?
What is alternation of generations?
cards.definition: The diploid sporophytic and haploid gametophytic phases alternate in the life cycle

cards.term: Which kingdom has multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes whose cells have no cell wall?
In what form do animals store food reserves?
What is the mode of nutrition of animals?
How do animals reproduce sexually?
cards.definition: Copulation of male and female, then embryological development

cards.term: Which organisms find no place in Whittaker's five kingdoms?
Why were viruses left out of classification?
cards.definition: They are not truly living: they have no cell structure

cards.term: What are viruses like outside a living cell?
What does the word 'virus' mean?
What did Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892) find about the cause of tobacco mosaic disease?
cards.definition: Microbes smaller than bacteria; they passed through bacteria-proof filters

cards.term: Who named the new pathogen 'virus' and called it Contagium vivum fluidum?
What does Contagium vivum fluidum mean?
What did W.M. Stanley (1935) show about viruses?
cards.definition: They can be crystallised; the crystals are largely proteins

cards.term: Can a virus reproduce outside a host cell?
Can a virus contain both RNA and DNA?
cards.definition: No. It has either RNA or DNA

cards.term: Which part of a virus is infectious?
Genetic material of viruses
cards.definition: Plant viruses: Single stranded RNA; Animal viruses: Single or double stranded RNA, or double stranded DNA; Bacteriophages: Double stranded DNA

cards.text: The protein coat of a virus, the {{c1::capsid}}, is made of small subunits called {{c2::capsomeres}}.

cards.term: In what geometric forms are capsomeres arranged?
Name five viral diseases of humans.
cards.definition: Mumps, small pox, herpes, influenza, AIDS

cards.term: Name four symptoms of viral infection in plants.
cards.definition:
• Mosaic formation
  • Leaf rolling and curling
  • Yellowing and vein clearing
  • Dwarfing, stunted growth

cards.term: Figure 2.6 (a) · Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV)
Figure 2.6 (b) · Bacteriophage
Who discovered viroids, and when?
Which disease do viroids cause?
How does a viroid differ from a virus?
cards.definition: A viroid is free RNA that lacks a protein coat

cards.term: What is a prion made of?
cards.definition: Abnormally folded protein, about the size of a virus

cards.text: Prions cause {{c1::bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE)}}, or mad cow disease, in cattle and {{c2::Creutzfeldt–Jacob disease (CJD)}} in humans.

cards.term: What are lichens?
cards.definition: Symbiotic associations between algae and fungi

cards.term: What is the algal partner of a lichen called?
What is the fungal partner of a lichen called?
What does each partner give the other in a lichen?
cards.definition: Alga: food. Fungus: shelter, plus mineral nutrients and water.

cards.term: Why are lichens good pollution indicators?
cards.definition: They do not grow in polluted areas
